10420:
Metaphorical means "not literally true, but used to describe something by comparing it to something else in order to make the meaning clearer, more vivid, or more powerful."

When you call something metaphorical, you are saying: this is not real or physical — it's a way of speaking that uses one idea to stand in for another.

To truly understand "metaphorical," you must first understand its opposite: literal.

Something is literal when it means exactly what it says — no more, no less. It refers to something real, physical, and factual.

Something is metaphorical when it doesn't mean what it literally says. Instead, it uses one thing to represent or describe another, because the comparison makes the meaning stronger.

Here is the clearest possible example of both, side by side:

Literal: "There is a fire in the kitchen."
(An actual fire is burning. Call the fire department.)

Metaphorical: "There is fire in her eyes."
(Her eyes are not actually on fire. It means her eyes show intense emotion — passion, anger, or determination.)

Notice what happened there. In the metaphorical version, the word "fire" was borrowed from its real-world meaning and placed into a new context to paint a picture of an emotion. Nobody expects you to fetch a bucket of water. Everyone understands it as a description.

That is what metaphorical means: using language as a picture rather than a fact.

As an adjective, "metaphorical" is used to describe a word, phrase, statement, or meaning that is being used figuratively — not literally.

You attach it to whatever you want to label as "not literal." For example:

  • "The word buried is being used in a metaphorical sense here." (Nobody is actually buried in dirt.)
  • "Her metaphorical cage was the routine she couldn't escape." (There is no physical cage.)
  • "That was a metaphorical punch to the gut." (Nobody was physically hit.)

In each case, "metaphorical" is a signal — a flag you raise to say: don't take this word or phrase at face value. Look deeper at what it's pointing to.

Here is something surprising: you use metaphorical language every single day without realizing it. The English language is absolutely packed with it.

When you say "I'm drowning in work," you don't mean you are literally underwater. You're using "drowning" metaphorically to describe being overwhelmed.

When you say "She has a warm personality," her skin temperature isn't unusually high. "Warm" is used metaphorically to mean kind and welcoming.

When you say "He climbed the corporate ladder," there is no physical ladder in an office. It's a metaphorical image for rising through the ranks of a company.

When you say "My heart is broken," the heart hasn't physically cracked. It's a metaphorical way of describing deep emotional pain.

All of these are metaphorical expressions — they borrow the image of a physical, tangible thing (water, warmth, a ladder, a broken object) and use it to describe something emotional, abstract, or invisible.

Because human beings often experience things — like emotions, ideas, or abstract situations — that are difficult to describe directly. There are no precise words for every shade of feeling or thought.

So we borrow. We take something everyone can see or touch and use it to describe something everyone can feel but not see. That is the whole power of metaphorical language. It makes the invisible, visible. It makes the abstract, concrete. It makes the complex, simple.

When someone says "he's a snake," you instantly understand they mean the person is deceptive and untrustworthy. A single metaphorical word did the work of a whole paragraph.

You will often hear or read the phrase "metaphorically speaking" (or "used metaphorically"). This is simply a way of flagging — before or after a statement — that you do not mean it literally.

"I could eat a horse right now — metaphorically speaking, of course."
(You are very hungry. You will not eat a horse.)

"He used 'battlefield' metaphorically — he was talking about the boardroom, not an actual war."

It's a clarification tool. It tells your listener: please interpret this as a comparison, not as a fact.
Metaphorical vs. Literal: A Quick Test

Whenever you want to check whether something is being used metaphorically, ask yourself one simple question:

"Is this actually, physically happening — or is this a comparison being used to describe something else?"

If it's physically happening → it's literal.
If it's a comparison pointing to something else → it's metaphorical.

"The office was a war zone." → Is there a real war being fought? No. → Metaphorical. (It means the office was chaotic and stressful.)

"The soldiers entered the war zone." → Is there a real war? Yes. → Literal.
One Last Nuance: Metaphorical Meanings That Become Normal

Over time, some metaphorical uses of words become so common that we stop thinking of them as metaphorical at all. They become the "normal" meaning of the word.

For example, the word "grasp" literally means to physically grab something with your hand. But when you say "I grasp what you mean," meaning you understand it, that is technically a metaphorical use — understanding is being compared to physically grabbing hold of something. We use it so routinely, though, that most people don't even notice the metaphor anymore.

These are called dead metaphors — metaphors so worn into everyday language that they no longer feel like comparisons. Examples include: "the foot of a hill," "the arm of a chair," "the mouth of a river," and "the leg of a journey." All borrowed from body parts, used metaphorically so long they simply became the standard words.

Metaphorical means: relating to or involving a comparison where one thing is described as another thing — not because it literally is that thing, but because the comparison captures something true and vivid about it. It is the opposite of literal. Metaphorical language is everywhere in daily speech, in literature, in business, and in art, because it is one of the most powerful tools human beings have for expressing ideas, emotions, and experiences that are otherwise hard to put into words.
10421:
If something is metaphysical, it belongs to a world beyond the physical — beyond what you can see, touch, weigh, measure, or test in a laboratory. It lives in the realm of pure thought, abstract reality, and fundamental existence.

Think of it this way: a rock is physical. You can hold it, describe it, study it scientifically. But the question of why anything exists at all — why there is a rock, or a universe, or you — rather than absolutely nothing? That question is metaphysical. It cannot be answered with a microscope or a ruler. It requires deep reasoning about the very nature of reality itself.

The word "metaphysical" carries two related but distinct senses. Understanding both will make you completely fluent with this word.

1. The Philosophical Sense

In philosophy, metaphysics is an entire field of study — the deepest, most fundamental branch of philosophy. It asks the biggest possible questions about existence and reality. So when something is called metaphysical in this sense, it means it belongs to this territory of foundational questions, such as:

  • What is reality, really? Is the physical world we see the only reality, or is there something deeper behind it?
  • What does it mean to exist? What is the difference between something that exists and something that doesn't?
  • What is time? Does it actually "flow," or is it just something our minds perceive?
  • What is identity? If you replace every single cell in a person's body, are they still the same person?
  • Do abstract things exist? Does the number "7" actually exist somewhere, or is it just an idea?
  • What is consciousness? Is your mind just your brain, or is there something more to it?

None of these questions can be answered purely by science or observation. They require pure reasoning at the deepest level. That is what makes them metaphysical.

When someone says, "That is a metaphysical question," they mean: this is not a question about facts you can observe — it is a question about the fundamental nature of reality, existence, or being.

2. The Broader, Everyday Sense

Outside strict philosophy, "metaphysical" is used more loosely to describe anything that is:

  • Abstract and beyond the physical world — not material, not tangible, not observable
  • Spiritual or supernatural — relating to forces, beings, or dimensions that lie beyond ordinary nature
  • Deeply theoretical — so abstract that it has no direct, concrete, practical consequence

In everyday speech, you will often hear people use "metaphysical" to describe spiritual beliefs, the soul, the afterlife, divine consciousness, or invisible forces governing the universe. A "metaphysical bookshop," for instance, typically sells books on spirituality, the occult, the soul, and consciousness — all things that exist beyond the measurable physical world.
The Heart of the Word: "Beyond Physical"

The most useful mental anchor is this: physical = of the material world, observable and measurable. Metaphysical = beyond that. Above it. Behind it. Deeper than it.

A broken leg is physical. The question of whether you have a soul is metaphysical.
The color of a flower is physical. The question of whether beauty is real or just a human perception is metaphysical.
Your brain activity is physical. The question of what consciousness actually is is metaphysical.

Notice the pattern: as soon as you step outside what science and physical observation can answer and enter the territory of fundamental reality, existence, being, and the abstract — you are in metaphysical territory.
How It Is Used in Sentences

Understanding a word fully means seeing it in action. Here are clear examples across different contexts:

  • "Whether God exists is a metaphysical question — it cannot be resolved by running an experiment."
  • "She had a metaphysical belief that the universe was conscious and aware of human lives."
  • "The philosopher argued that numbers are metaphysical entities — they don't exist in physical space, yet they are somehow real."
  • "His poetry moved beyond the personal and entered metaphysical territory, exploring the nature of time and eternity."
  • "The debate over free will is one of the oldest metaphysical debates in history."

You will sometimes encounter the term Metaphysical Poets when studying English literature. This refers to a group of 17th-century English poets — most famously John Donne — whose poetry was known for exploring abstract, spiritual, and philosophical ideas (love, death, God, the soul) alongside intense intellectual analysis and surprising comparisons. Their work was called "metaphysical" because it constantly reached beyond the physical and the obvious into the abstract and the spiritual. If you ever read literature, knowing this connection will serve you well.

This is important, because the word is sometimes misused:

  • It does not simply mean strange or weird, even though people sometimes use it that way carelessly.
  • It does not mean psychological (which relates to the mind and behavior, not to the fundamental nature of reality).
  • It does not mean theoretical in the simple scientific sense. A physicist theorizing about black holes is being scientific, not metaphysical — because the theory still relates to the physical universe and could in principle be tested.

Something is genuinely metaphysical only when it steps outside the territory of physical observation and empirical testing entirely, and enters the realm of fundamental questions about existence, reality, being, or what lies beyond the physical.

Metaphysical means relating to things that lie beyond the physical and observable world — the deep, abstract, fundamental questions about what exists, what reality truly is, and what (if anything) lies beyond the material universe.

Master that, and you have fully mastered this word.
10422:
Metaphysics (noun) is a branch of philosophy that investigates the most fundamental questions about the nature of reality. Not how reality works — science handles that — but what reality is, at its deepest possible level. It asks questions like: What exists? What is time, really? Do we have free will? What is the mind?

If you think of human knowledge as a building, science occupies most of the floors. But metaphysics is the foundation — it examines the ground the entire building rests on.

The word is used as a singular noun, even though it ends in "-s," just like "physics" or "mathematics." You say "metaphysics is a difficult subject," not "metaphysics are."
Why Metaphysics Is Necessary (and Why Science Alone Isn't Enough)

Science is magnificent at answering "How does this work?" questions. Physics explains gravity. Neuroscience explains how neurons fire. Chemistry explains how atoms bond.

But notice: before you can study existing things, you have to understand what existence means. Before you can measure time, you have to understand what time actually is. Before you can study the brain, you have to think about whether the mind is the same thing as the brain or something more.

These questions aren't unanswered just because scientists haven't gotten around to them. They are structurally beyond what observation and experiment can resolve on their own, because they are questions about the very framework within which science operates. Metaphysics is the discipline that takes these questions seriously and tries to answer them through careful reasoning and logical analysis.

Metaphysics is not one narrow question — it is a family of deeply related questions about the bedrock of reality. Here are its central areas:

What exists? (Ontology)

The most central part of metaphysics is called ontology, which is the study of being and existence. Its core question is: what kinds of things genuinely exist?

This sounds easy until you think about it. Does the number 7 exist? You can't touch it or weigh it. But it certainly seems to be true that seven apples are seven, not six or eight — so "7" seems to have some kind of reality. Does it exist the same way an apple exists, or in a different, non-physical way? What about your emotions — does love "exist" in the same sense your brain does?

Ontology also tackles a bigger version of this: is everything that exists physical — made of matter and energy — or do some non-physical things (like minds, mathematical objects, or moral facts) genuinely exist too?

What is the nature of space and time?

Is time real, or is it an illusion produced by our minds? Does the past still exist somewhere, or is it truly gone forever? Does the future already exist in some sense, waiting to be reached, or is it yet to be created? Is space merely the gap between objects, or is it a real, independent thing that would still exist even if the universe were completely empty?

These are not questions physics alone can answer, because they're questions about what space and time fundamentally are, not just questions about how they behave.

What is the relationship between the mind and the body?

You have a brain — a physical structure made of neurons, chemicals, and electrical signals. You also have a mind — thoughts, feelings, memories, and above all, conscious experience: the felt sense of seeing the color red, tasting coffee, feeling joy or pain.

The question is: what is the relationship between these two things? Is your mind simply what your brain does, so that a complete understanding of neuroscience would be a complete understanding of you? Or is there something about conscious experience that can never be fully explained in physical terms? This is called the mind-body problem, and it is one of the most debated questions in all of metaphysics.

What is causation?

When a moving billiard ball strikes a stationary one and sends it rolling, we say the first ball caused the second to move. But what exactly is causation? Is it a real feature built into the fabric of the universe, or is it just a pattern our minds recognize in events that happen to follow one another in sequence? Does every event have a cause? Could something ever happen for absolutely no reason at all? These are metaphysical questions — and the answers have enormous implications for science, religion, and everyday reasoning.

What makes something the same thing over time?

Here is a famous thought experiment. Imagine a ship. Over the course of many years, every single plank is replaced, one at a time, with a new one. At the end, not one original piece of wood remains. Is it still the same ship? This is the "Ship of Theseus" problem.

Now apply it to yourself. Nearly every atom in your body has been replaced since you were a child. Your beliefs, memories, and personality have all changed. So what makes you the same person you were ten years ago? What is personal identity? What makes anything persist as the same thing over time? Metaphysics tackles this directly.

Do we have free will?

If the universe operates according to laws of cause and effect — and if every event is the product of prior events going all the way back to the beginning of the universe — then isn't every decision you make simply the inevitable result of prior causes that you had no control over? Did you truly choose to read this, or was your "choice" just the mechanical outcome of your brain state, which was shaped by your history, which was shaped by causes before you were born?

If free will doesn't exist, what does that mean for moral responsibility — for praise, blame, punishment, and justice? This is a metaphysical question with enormous consequences for ethics and law.

What is the ultimate nature of reality?

Does God exist? If so, what is God's nature? Is the universe infinite or finite? Could there be realities beyond this one — other universes, other dimensions? Is there any purpose or meaning built into the structure of reality, or is the universe entirely indifferent and purposeless? These cosmological and theological questions also fall within metaphysics.

Both metaphysics and religion ask big, ultimate questions about existence, God, and the nature of reality. The crucial difference is in method.

Religion typically starts from faith — from texts, revelation, or spiritual authority — and accepts certain truths without requiring them to be logically proven.

Metaphysics insists on rational argument. Even when a metaphysician is investigating whether God exists, they demand rigorous logical reasoning, precise definitions, and arguments that anyone can examine and challenge. Faith is not a method in metaphysics. Everything must be defended with reasons that can withstand scrutiny.

Metaphysics might seem like an abstract luxury, disconnected from real life. But hidden metaphysical assumptions quietly shape almost everything we think and do.

When you hold someone responsible for a crime, you are assuming they had free will — a metaphysical position. When you trust that your memories connect you to your past self, you are relying on a theory of personal identity. When doctors treat a patient today as the same person they treated last year, they are making a metaphysical assumption about identity over time. When science proceeds on the assumption that there is a real, external physical world that exists independently of anyone's mind — that too is a metaphysical claim (one that, remarkably, not all philosophers accept).

Metaphysics doesn't just float above real life. It underpins it invisibly, and getting it right matters for science, ethics, law, religion, and self-understanding.

Metaphysics, as a noun, names the branch of philosophy that asks the deepest possible questions about reality — questions that science alone cannot fully answer because they concern the very framework reality is built on. Its core areas include the study of existence (what is real and in what sense), the nature of time and space, the relationship between mind and body, the meaning of causation, personal identity over time, free will, and the ultimate structure of the cosmos. It proceeds entirely through rigorous reasoning and logical argument, not faith or experiment. And though its questions can feel abstract, they quietly form the foundation of nearly every serious thing human beings think and believe.
10423: To metastasize means to spread from one place to other places in a harmful way, taking root and growing in those new places. It is almost always used about disease — especially cancer — and sometimes used figuratively about the spread of harmful things.

When a doctor says cancer has metastasized, it means the cancer has done something very dangerous: it has escaped from where it started and traveled to other parts of the body, where it begins growing all over again.

Think of it this way. Imagine a fire starts in one room of a house. If it stays there, firefighters can focus on that one room. But if sparks fly out and start new fires in the kitchen, the bedroom, and the attic — all burning independently — it becomes far harder to fight. That is essentially what happens when cancer metastasizes.

Here is the step-by-step picture of what the word actually describes:

Some cancer cells break away from the original tumor (called the primary tumor). These cells then enter the bloodstream or the lymphatic system (the body's fluid-drainage network) and travel through the body like passengers on a highway. When they reach a new organ — the lungs, the liver, the brain, the bones — they settle in, multiply, and form a brand-new tumor there. That new tumor is called a metastasis (or metastases in the plural). The act of all this happening is what we call metastasizing.

One critical detail — and this is something many people don't know — the new tumor is still the same type of cancer as the original. If someone has breast cancer and it metastasizes to the lungs, the tumors in the lungs are made of breast cancer cells, not lung cancer cells. Doctors even call it "metastatic breast cancer in the lungs," not "lung cancer." This matters enormously for treatment, because the cells behave like their origin, not like their new location.
Who or What Does the Metastasizing?

Grammatically, the subject of this verb is the disease or the cancer cells themselves — not the person.

You would say:

  • "The cancer metastasized to her liver." (The cancer did the spreading.)
  • "His melanoma had metastasized throughout his lymph nodes."
  • "Doctors feared the tumor would metastasize."
  • "By the time it was detected, it had already metastasized."

You would not say "She metastasized" — the person doesn't metastasize, the cancer does.
Why This Word Carries Such Weight

In medicine, metastasizing is what makes cancer so much more dangerous and so much harder to cure. A localized tumor (one that has not metastasized) can sometimes be fully removed with surgery. But once a cancer metastasizes, there are now multiple sites of disease throughout the body, and surgery alone is rarely enough. This is why, when someone is diagnosed with cancer, one of the first and most urgent questions is: Has it metastasized? The answer dramatically changes the outlook and the treatment plan.

Because the medical image is so powerful — something harmful quietly spreading, taking hold in new places, growing out of control — the word is regularly borrowed for non-medical situations. When writers, journalists, or thinkers want to describe how something bad spreads from one place and corrupts or overtakes other places, they use "metastasize" to convey that gravity.

Examples:

  • "The corruption that began in one department slowly metastasized across the entire organization."
  • "A local conflict had metastasized into a regional war."
  • "Misinformation can metastasize rapidly on social media."

In all these cases, the word is doing the same work: something harmful that started in one place has spread outward, established itself in new places, and is now far harder to contain than it would have been at the start. The figurative use always carries the medical word's dark undertone — that this spreading is dangerous, possibly uncontrollable, and very bad news.

Since you'll encounter these in the same conversations:

  • Metastasis (noun) — the process itself, or a single secondary tumor. "The scan revealed a metastasis in the brain."
  • Metastases (noun, plural) — multiple secondary tumors. "She had metastases in three organs."
  • Metastatic (adjective) — describing cancer that has already spread. "He was diagnosed with metastatic prostate cancer."
  • Metastasizing (present participle) — the ongoing act. "The disease is still metastasizing."
  • Metastasized (past tense / past participle) — it already happened. "By then, it had metastasized."

To metastasize means for something harmful — almost always cancer — to spread from its original location to other parts of the body (or, figuratively, to other areas of life), establishing itself there and continuing to grow, making the problem far larger and harder to stop than it was before.
10424:
As a noun, mete means a boundary, a limit, or a boundary marker — specifically, a fixed point or line that marks where a piece of land ends.

Think of it as an invisible (or sometimes physical) line drawn on the ground that says: "This far, and no further." Beyond that line, the land belongs to someone else, or simply ceases to be the land in question.
Where You'll Actually See This Word

The noun form of mete is rare in everyday speech. It survives almost exclusively in one important legal and surveying context:

"Metes and bounds"

This is a centuries-old system used to describe the exact boundaries of a piece of land — the kind you'd still find in old land deeds, legal property documents, and real estate records, especially in the United States.

  • Metes = the measured boundaries of the land — described as distances and directions (e.g., "100 feet heading northeast").
  • Bounds = natural or established landmarks that form the border — like a river, a road, a tree, or a stone wall.

Together, metes and bounds give a complete, precise picture of where a plot of land begins and ends.

Example sentence:
"The deed described the property according to its metes and bounds, beginning at the old oak tree at the north corner."

Long ago, mete also existed as a noun meaning food or a meal. This meaning has been completely absorbed into the modern word "meat" — which, interestingly, originally meant any food at all, not just animal flesh. Over centuries, "meat" narrowed to its current meaning, and the standalone noun mete for food disappeared entirely from use.

You may occasionally encounter this old meaning in very old poetry, religious texts, or archaic literature — but outside of those contexts, it's extinct. You don't need to use or remember it for practical purposes.
The Key Distinction: Noun vs. Verb

It helps to know that mete is far more commonly encountered as a verb — meaning to distribute or to deal out — as in the phrase "mete out punishment." The noun form is much rarer and more specialized.

So if you see mete standing alone as a noun, it almost certainly refers to a boundary or limit — most likely in a legal or land-surveying context.

As a noun today:A boundary, limit, or boundary marker for a piece of land
Main surviving use:The legal phrase "metes and bounds"
Archaic noun use:Food or meal (now extinct; evolved into "meat")
Don't confuse with:The verb mete (to deal out or distribute)

The noun mete is a quiet, specialized word — not one you'll use in daily conversation, but one that carries precision and historical weight in legal and property contexts.
10425:
To mete out something means to give or deliver something to someone — especially a punishment, a reward, or a form of treatment — in a deliberate and decided way.

The person or authority doing the "meting out" has made a conscious decision about what to give and how much, and then carries it out.

Think of it like a judge sitting down, carefully deciding what sentence a criminal deserves, and then delivering it. That act of deciding and delivering — that's "meting out."

Two things are almost always true when "mete out" is used:

1. There is a power difference.
The one who metes something out is always in a position of authority or power over the one receiving it. A judge, a government, a god, a parent, a school, a military commander — these are the kinds of figures who "mete out." You wouldn't say a friend "meted out" a gift to you casually. The word carries weight and authority.

2. It is deliberate and considered.
"Mete out" is never accidental. It suggests that someone thought about it, made a judgment, and then acted. There is an intentional quality to it — almost like measuring out what is deserved.

Most commonly, mete out is used with:

  • Punishment (by far the most common use)
  • Justice
  • Discipline
  • Sentences (legal sentences)
  • Harsh treatment
  • Consequences
  • Rewards or praise (less common, but possible)

The word leans heavily toward negative things — punishment, discipline, harsh sentences. When used with positive things like praise or rewards, it often sounds ironic or overly formal.

Here are examples that show how the word works in real sentences:

  • "The judge meted out a ten-year prison sentence to the convicted man."

The judge decided what the criminal deserved and delivered it.

  • "The school meted out severe punishment to the students who cheated on the exam."

The school authority deliberately decided and applied consequences.

  • "History has meted out harsh judgment to leaders who abused their power."

Here, "history" is treated poetically as an authority that passes judgment over time.

  • "The coach meted out extra training sessions as punishment for the players who broke the rules."

The coach, in a position of power, decided and imposed a consequence.

  • "The government was accused of meting out brutal treatment to protesters."

Notice how it works with treatment, not just formal sentences.

"Mete out" is a formal expression. You won't hear it in casual, everyday conversation. It belongs in:

  • Newspapers and journalism
  • Legal or official writing
  • Literary writing
  • Serious discussions about justice, law, or morality

You would never say "My mom meted out some snacks to us" — it would sound strange because the situation isn't serious enough. But "My mom meted out chores as punishment" works, because it involves a deliberate, authority-driven consequence.
How It's Different from Similar Words

"Give" is neutral — it has no sense of authority, judgment, or weight. "He gave him a punishment" sounds almost accidental. "He meted out a punishment" sounds deliberate and authoritative.

"Impose" is close in meaning, but "impose" emphasizes the forcing of something on someone. "Mete out" emphasizes the measured deciding and delivering of something.

"Administer" (as in "administer punishment") is also similar, but more clinical and procedural — like following a process. "Mete out" carries more of a sense of judgment and weight.

• The structure is: Subject + mete out + object
  • It can also take a "to" phrase: Subject + mete out + object + to + recipient

"The court meted out the sentence."
"The court meted out the sentence to the defendant."

  • Past tense: meted out
  • Present: metes out
  • Continuous: meting out
One-Line Summary to Lock It In

"Mete out" means to deliberately decide and deliver something — usually a punishment or consequence — from a position of authority, in a way that feels measured and intentional.

If you ever see it in a sentence, ask yourself: Who's in charge here, and what are they deliberately giving to someone as a result of a judgment? That's always what "mete out" is about.
10426:
Metempsychosis is the belief that when a living creature dies, its soul does not die along with it. Instead, the soul survives death, exits the old body, and enters a brand new body — beginning a fresh life. This cycle of death and rebirth repeats over and over, potentially across hundreds or even thousands of lifetimes.

Think of it with this image: imagine the soul as a flame inside a lantern. When the lantern breaks and is destroyed, the flame does not go out — it is carefully carried over and placed inside a new lantern. The old lantern is gone forever, but the flame burns on. Metempsychosis says the soul works exactly like that flame.
The soul can enter any kind of body — not just human

This is one of the most striking and important features of metempsychosis: the soul is not limited to being reborn as a human. Depending on how the previous life was lived, the soul could next inhabit the body of an animal, a bird, an insect, or even — in some traditions — a plant.

This means that according to this belief, the beggar on the street may have once been a king, and the stray dog wandering the alley may carry the soul of someone who lived selfishly in a past life. Every living thing, under this doctrine, is potentially a soul at some stage of its journey.
What determines where the soul goes next?

In almost every tradition that holds this belief, the soul's next destination is not random — it is earned. The force that determines the direction of the soul's next birth is most commonly called karma, a word from ancient Indian philosophy meaning something like "the moral weight of your actions."

In simple terms: if you lived a good, ethical, compassionate life, your soul earns a better or higher rebirth. If you lived selfishly, cruelly, or harmfully, your soul descends to a lower form of life in the next birth. The soul is, in a sense, serving out the consequences of its own past behaviour.

The ultimate ambition in most traditions that teach metempsychosis is not simply to be reborn into a better life — it is to escape the cycle entirely. After enough lifetimes of spiritual growth, purification, and wisdom, the soul is believed to reach a state of liberation where it no longer needs to be reborn at all. In Hinduism, this final liberation is called moksha. In Buddhism, it is called nirvana.
Metempsychosis vs. reincarnation — is there a difference?

These two words are frequently used interchangeably, and for most everyday purposes they mean the same thing. However, there is a subtle distinction worth being aware of.

Reincarnation, taken literally, means re-entering the flesh — and in popular usage, it tends to imply being reborn specifically as a human being. Metempsychosis is the broader, older, more formal philosophical term, and it explicitly includes transmigration into animals and plants, not just humans. So metempsychosis is the wider concept: every reincarnation is a form of metempsychosis, but not every metempsychosis is a reincarnation in the narrower sense.

A third related term you may encounter is transmigration of souls, which is simply a plain English way of describing the same idea — the soul migrating (travelling) from one body to another.

Ancient Greek philosophy is where the word itself was born, and some of Greece's greatest thinkers embraced the idea passionately.

Pythagoras — the mathematician famous for his geometric theorem — was among the most fervent believers. He claimed to remember his own past lives, including a life as a warrior in the Trojan War. He refused to eat beans, reportedly because he believed they might contain the souls of the dead. Plato, one of history's greatest philosophers, also wrote extensively about the soul's journey between lives. In his dialogue Phaedo, he argues that the soul is immortal and cycles through many bodies. In The Republic, he describes souls choosing their next life before being born — like travellers picking their next destination.

Hinduism gives this idea its richest and most developed expression. The endless cycle of birth, death, and rebirth is called samsara (meaning "wandering through"). The soul — called the atman — transmigrates from body to body, lifetime after lifetime, guided by karma. The goal of Hindu spiritual practice is ultimately to achieve moksha, the liberation of the soul from samsara, at which point the individual soul merges back into the universal divine reality (Brahman).

Buddhism has a more carefully nuanced position. The Buddha explicitly rejected the idea of a fixed, eternal, unchanging soul (which he called atman). Buddhism instead speaks of a stream of consciousness or a flow of karma that continues after death and shapes the next birth — but it insists there is no solid "thing" called a soul doing the travelling. This is why Buddhist rebirth is technically distinct from metempsychosis, even though in everyday conversation the two are often discussed together. The destination of rebirth in Buddhism can be one of several realms — not just the human world, but also animal, hellish, or heavenly realms — and the goal is likewise to reach nirvana, escaping the cycle.

Jainism, another ancient Indian religion, also teaches metempsychosis. In Jain belief, every living being — including tiny insects and even plants — possesses a soul. These souls transmigrate through countless forms of life, accumulating or shedding karma, with the ultimate aim of achieving liberation.

The Orphic tradition, a religious movement in ancient Greece, also taught metempsychosis. The Orphics believed that the soul was originally divine but had fallen and become imprisoned in a cycle of mortal bodies as a kind of punishment or purification. Through ritual, spiritual discipline, and righteous living across multiple lifetimes, the soul could gradually purify itself and eventually return to its divine origin.
One important nuance: memory is not carried over

In almost all versions of this belief, when the soul enters its new body and a new life begins, it does not bring its memories from the previous life. You are born fresh — you do not remember being a Roman senator, a sparrow, or a medieval farmer in past lives.

What is carried forward, however, is subtler and more important: the moral and spiritual consequences of past actions (karma), as well as deep character tendencies, inclinations, and the overall level of spiritual development the soul has reached. In this sense, who you are in this life — your temperament, your instincts, your natural gifts and struggles — may, according to this doctrine, be partly the accumulated residue of everything you have been in every life before.

The word metempsychosis appears in one of the greatest novels ever written — Ulysses by James Joyce. In an early scene, the main character Leopold Bloom finds a book belonging to his wife Molly with the word "metempsychosis" in it. She asks him what it means, and he explains it as the transmigration of souls, adding the simple example that the ancient Greeks thought "you could be changed into an animal or a tree." Molly immediately replies: "O, rocks! Tell us in plain words." — a response that perfectly captures why the word, despite describing a universal human idea, sounds so formidably technical.

Metempsychosis is the philosophical and spiritual doctrine that the soul is immortal and, upon the death of one body, travels into and inhabits a new body — which may belong to a human, an animal, or a plant. This cycle of rebirth repeats across many lifetimes, typically governed by the moral law of karma. The soul's ultimate goal, in most traditions that teach this, is to grow spiritually across lifetimes until it finally achieves liberation and escapes the cycle of rebirth altogether. It is, in the most fundamental sense, the formal name for one of humanity's oldest and most widespread ideas: that death is not an ending, but a transition — a door through which the soul steps from one chapter of its existence into the next.
10427:
A meteor is the bright streak of light you see flashing across the night sky — what most people casually call a "shooting star" or "falling star." It is not a star at all. It is the glowing trail produced when a small piece of rock or metal from outer space enters Earth's atmosphere at very high speed and burns up.

The light itself lasts only a fraction of a second to a few seconds, and then it's gone.
The essential trio: meteoroid → meteor → meteorite

To fully understand "meteor," you need to know the three related words, because they describe the same object at different stages of its journey.

Meteoroid — the rock (or chunk of metal) while it is still floating in outer space. It could be as tiny as a grain of sand or as large as a small boulder.

Meteor — the event and the light. The moment that same rock enters Earth's atmosphere and burns up, producing a streak of light — that streak, that glow, that flash — is called a meteor. So a meteor is technically not the rock itself. It is the light phenomenon caused by the rock.

Meteorite — if the rock is large enough and doesn't completely burn up, a chunk of it survives and falls to the ground. That surviving piece, now resting on Earth's surface, is called a meteorite.

Think of it this way:

  • Rock floating in space → meteoroid
  • Rock entering atmosphere, burning up, creating a streak of light → meteor
  • Rock that survives and lands on Earth → meteorite

Most rocks that enter the atmosphere are so small they burn up completely. They never become meteorites.
What actually causes the streak of light

When a meteoroid enters Earth's atmosphere, it is traveling at an enormous speed — typically between 11 and 72 kilometres per second. That is tens of thousands of kilometres per hour.

At those speeds, the rock collides violently with air molecules. This causes two things: the air in front of the rock gets intensely compressed and heated, and the surface of the rock itself gets scorched and vaporized. This superheated gas and vaporized rock material glows brilliantly — producing the streak of light we call a meteor.

This all happens at a height of roughly 80 to 120 kilometres above Earth's surface — far above where airplanes fly.

A meteor appears as a sudden, fast-moving streak of white, yellow, orange, or even greenish light across the sky. It moves much faster than any airplane and disappears quickly. Some leave a faint glowing trail behind them for a few seconds, called a persistent train. Others flash and vanish almost instantly.

The brightness varies widely. A faint meteor might be barely visible, while a brilliant one can briefly light up the entire sky. In fact, any meteor brighter than the planet Venus (one of the brightest objects in the night sky) is given a special name: a fireball. An exceptionally violent fireball that explodes in the atmosphere is called a bolide.

Stars are enormous balls of burning gas located unimaginably far from Earth. A shooting star has nothing to do with actual stars. The name exists simply because, to ancient observers, it looked like a star moving across the sky. The accurate name is meteor.

On most nights, you might spot a handful of random meteors if you watch the sky long enough. These are called sporadic meteors — they come from meteoroids drifting alone through space in no particular pattern.

However, several times each year, Earth passes through a dense stream of debris left behind by a comet (a comet is an icy body that sheds material as it orbits the Sun). When Earth moves through this debris cloud, dozens or even hundreds of meteors per hour can be visible. This event is called a meteor shower.

During a meteor shower, all the meteors appear to radiate outward from a single point in the sky (called the radiant). This is a perspective effect — the meteoroids are actually travelling in parallel paths, but just like train tracks appear to converge in the distance, the meteors seem to come from one point.

Meteor showers happen on predictable dates each year because Earth crosses the same debris streams at the same points in its orbit. Some well-known ones include:

  • Perseids — peak around mid-August, one of the most reliable and active showers
  • Leonids — peak around mid-November, known for occasional spectacular outbursts
  • Geminids — peak around mid-December, one of the strongest showers of the year

Showers are named after the constellation where their radiant point appears to be located.

It is estimated that tens of thousands of tonnes of meteoritic material fall to Earth every year — but almost all of it is microscopic dust. Objects large enough to produce a visible meteor are far rarer. Still, on any given clear night, a patient observer can spot several meteors per hour simply by watching the sky.

The vast majority burn up entirely in the atmosphere and pose no danger. Only objects larger than roughly a metre in diameter are likely to survive and reach the ground as meteorites, and that happens far less frequently.
When "meteor" is used in a sentence

• "We stayed up late to watch the meteor shower."
  • "I saw a bright meteor streak across the sky last night."
  • "Scientists study meteor impacts to understand the early solar system."

In everyday speech, people sometimes loosely say "a meteor hit the ground" — but strictly speaking, once it hits the ground, it becomes a meteorite. In casual conversation this is widely understood and accepted, but in scientific contexts the distinction matters.
A meteor is the streak of light produced when a piece of space rock burns up as it speeds through Earth's atmosphere — commonly called a shooting star, though it has nothing to do with stars.
10428: "Meteoric" has two layers of meaning — a literal one and a figurative one. In everyday life, you will almost always encounter it in its figurative sense, but understanding the literal sense first makes the figurative one click instantly.

A meteor is a rock from outer space that enters Earth's atmosphere and burns up as it falls. As it does, it produces a streak of extremely bright, intense light across the sky — appearing and disappearing in seconds. It's the blazing speed and the spectacular, eye-catching brightness that define a meteor.

In its literal sense, "meteoric" simply means of or relating to meteors. For example, scientists might talk about meteoric dust (tiny particles from meteors) or meteoric iron (metal found in meteorites that landed on Earth). This literal use is mostly found in scientific writing.
The Figurative Meaning (The One You'll Use Most)

This is where the word truly lives. In figurative use, "meteoric" describes something that happens or develops with breathtaking speed, intensity, and impressiveness — just like the blazing streak of a meteor across the sky.

When you call something meteoric, you are saying three things at once:

  • It happened extremely fast
  • It was dramatic and spectacular — not quiet or gradual
  • It was striking enough to make people notice, the way a meteor makes heads turn

It is most often used to describe a person's rise in status, fame, power, or success. For example:

"She had a meteoric rise to fame."

This means she went from being unknown to being very famous in a shockingly short amount of time — and the process was dramatic and impressive, not slow and steady.

1. It is about HOW fast, not just THAT something is fast.
"Meteoric" is a strong, dramatic word. It doesn't just mean "quick." It means astonishingly quick — the kind of speed that makes people stop and say "Wow, that happened fast." A career that grows steadily over ten years is not meteoric. A career that explodes in two years is.

2. It often carries a hidden shadow of brevity.
Real meteors are spectacular but short-lived — they burn bright and vanish in seconds. Because of this, "meteoric" often quietly hints that the rapid success might not last, or that the person burned themselves out along the way. This isn't always the intended meaning, but the word carries this undercurrent. A writer might choose "meteoric" specifically to suggest that someone's sudden fame was brilliant but unsustainable.

However — and this is important — in modern everyday usage, many people use "meteoric" simply to mean very fast and impressive, without intending any hint of a coming downfall. Context will tell you which way it's being used.

3. It almost always describes the upward journey, not a downfall.
"Meteoric rise" is one of the most common phrases in the English language. You will rarely see "meteoric fall." Even though real meteors literally fall from the sky, the word "meteoric" in English has become fixed as a symbol of dramatic upward movement and success. Think of it as borrowed from the image of the blazing light shooting across the sky — not from the physical direction of the rock.

• It does not mean simply big or impressive on its own. A famous landmark is not "meteoric." A historical empire is not "meteoric" just because it was powerful. The word always needs that element of sudden speed.
  • It does not mean ordinary fast. You would not say "the car moved at a meteoric speed" to describe normal highway driving. The word is reserved for truly exceptional, jaw-dropping speed of change.
Where You Will See It Used

"Meteoric" almost always appears attached to words about growth, success, or careers:

  • Meteoric rise — the most common phrase; used for people climbing to fame, power, or success very quickly
  • Meteoric career — a career that shot upward at astonishing speed
  • Meteoric ascent — same idea as meteoric rise, slightly more formal
  • Meteoric success — success that arrived suddenly and dramatically
  • Meteoric growth — used for businesses, movements, or ideas that expand at explosive speed

If someone says an athlete had a meteoric rise, picture a young person who was completely unknown two years ago and is now a global superstar. That speed, that drama, that sense of "where did this person come from?" — that is exactly what "meteoric" captures.

If a tech startup had meteoric growth, it went from a small idea in someone's garage to a billion-dollar company in a very short window of time — in a way that shocked even industry experts.

The word always points to the same feeling: something blazed across the scene so fast and so brilliantly that people could barely believe it.
10429: A meteorite is a natural, solid object from outer space that has traveled through Earth's atmosphere and landed on Earth's surface. It is a piece of rock, metal, or a mixture of both — originally floating in space — that survived a fiery journey through the sky and made it all the way to the ground.
Understanding the Full Journey (Meteoroid → Meteor → Meteorite)

To truly understand what a meteorite is, you need to know that the same object goes by three different names depending on where it is:

1. Meteoroid (in space)
When a chunk of rock or metal is drifting through outer space, it is called a meteoroid (if it's small, up to about 1 metre). Larger objects in space are called asteroids. Meteoroids are usually broken-off fragments from asteroids, or occasionally from comets.

2. Meteor (in the atmosphere, burning)
When a meteoroid enters Earth's atmosphere, it collides with air molecules at extremely high speed — often tens of kilometres per second. This friction generates intense heat, causing the object's outer surface to glow and vaporise. You see this as a brief, bright streak of light in the night sky. That glowing streak is a meteor — what people casually call a "shooting star" or "falling star." Note: it isn't actually a star at all.

Most meteoroids are small (the size of a grain of sand or a pebble) and burn up completely in the atmosphere, leaving nothing behind on the ground.

3. Meteorite (on the ground)
If the object is large enough to survive the fiery passage through the atmosphere without completely burning up, and it lands on the ground — that object is now called a meteorite. The same rock was a meteoroid in space, a meteor while glowing in the sky, and becomes a meteorite the moment it reaches the surface.
What a Meteorite Looks Like

The Fusion Crust

One of the most distinctive features of a freshly fallen meteorite is its fusion crust — a thin, dark (usually black or dark brown), glassy outer shell. As the meteorite's surface melted during its atmospheric entry and then rapidly cooled, it solidified into this smooth, sometimes shiny crust. It is typically only about 1 millimetre thick. This crust is one of the key features scientists use to recognise a meteorite.

Over time (months to years), the fusion crust weathers away, making older meteorites harder to identify.

Size and Weight

Meteorites come in a huge range of sizes:

  • Micrometeorites: Dust-sized particles, too small to see with the naked eye, that silently rain down on Earth constantly.
  • Small meteorites: Pebble- to fist-sized objects.
  • Large meteorites: The size of a car or bigger.
  • The largest known meteorite on Earth: The Hoba meteorite in Namibia, Africa. It weighs approximately 60 tonnes (60,000 kg) and is still sitting right where it landed, embedded in the ground. It has never been moved.

Iron-containing meteorites are notably heavier than ordinary rocks of the same size, which is another clue to their identity.
The Three Main Types of Meteorites

Scientists classify meteorites into three broad categories based on what they're made of:

1. Stony Meteorites (Most Common — ~86%)

These are made mostly of silicate minerals, meaning they are primarily rock. They look similar to ordinary Earth rocks, which makes them the hardest to identify unless you know what to look for.

Stony meteorites are divided into two groups:

  • Chondrites: The most primitive and most common type. They are named after tiny, spherical structures within them called chondrules — small droplets of molten rock that solidified very early in the history of the solar system, about 4.567 billion years ago. Chondrites are essentially unchanged since the solar system formed, making them priceless scientific time capsules.
  • Achondrites: Stony meteorites that do not contain chondrules. These come from bodies that were once geologically active — places like the Moon, Mars, or larger asteroids that melted and differentiated (separated into layers) long ago. Lunar and Martian meteorites fall into this category.

2. Iron Meteorites (~5%)

These are made almost entirely of iron and nickel, a metallic alloy. They are very dense and feel much heavier than an ordinary rock of the same size. When you slice one open and etch the cross-section with acid, it reveals a beautiful, crystalline geometric pattern called the Widmanstätten pattern — a structure that forms only when molten metal cools over millions of years. No human process can replicate it. Iron meteorites come from the cores of large asteroids that melted and solidified billions of years ago.

3. Stony-Iron Meteorites (Rarest — ~1%)

These contain roughly equal parts rock and metal. The most visually stunning subtype is the pallasite: a metallic iron-nickel framework embedded with translucent, gem-like crystals of the mineral olivine (which can be yellow-green to yellow-brown). When sliced thin and held up to light, they look like stained glass. Pallasites are thought to come from the boundary between the metal core and rocky mantle of differentiated asteroids.
Where Do Meteorites Come From?

The vast majority come from the asteroid belt — a region between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter, filled with millions of rocky and metallic bodies left over from the formation of the solar system. Collisions in the asteroid belt sometimes knock fragments out of their orbits, sending them on paths toward Earth.

A small number come from the Moon. Large impacts on the Moon blast rocks off its surface, and some of those rocks eventually fall to Earth as lunar meteorites.

An even smaller number come from Mars. Giant asteroid impacts on Mars have ejected rocks into space, and some have made their way to Earth after millions of years. These are called Martian meteorites (or SNC meteorites). We can confirm they're from Mars because the gases trapped inside them match the composition of Mars's atmosphere, measured directly by NASA's Viking landers.

A tiny fraction may originate from comets, though this is much harder to confirm.
Impact Craters

When a very large meteorite hits Earth at high speed, the energy released is enormous. The impact excavates a bowl-shaped depression in the ground called a meteorite impact crater (or astrobleme for ancient, eroded ones).

A famous example is Meteor Crater (also called Barringer Crater) in Arizona, USA — about 1.2 km wide and 170 metres deep, formed roughly 50,000 years ago by an iron meteorite perhaps 50 metres across.

The most consequential impact in recent Earth history is the one that occurred about 66 million years ago near what is now Chicxulub, Mexico. The impactor was an asteroid roughly 10–15 km wide. The impact released energy billions of times greater than any nuclear weapon, triggering wildfires, a "nuclear winter" from dust and debris blocking sunlight, and ultimately contributing to the mass extinction of about 75% of all species on Earth — including most of the non-avian dinosaurs.
Where Are Meteorites Found?

Meteorites fall randomly all over Earth, but they are far more likely to be discovered in certain places:

  • Antarctica: The cold, dry conditions preserve meteorites extremely well. Glacial ice flow concentrates them in certain areas. Tens of thousands of meteorites have been collected here.
  • Hot deserts (Sahara, Arabian Desert, Atacama, Nullarbor Plain in Australia): The dry conditions preserve them, and they stand out visually against light-coloured sand or rock.

In other environments, most meteorites are quickly weathered away or simply go unnoticed, looking like ordinary stones.
Scientific Importance

Meteorites are among the most scientifically valuable objects on Earth. Here's why:

  • They are the oldest solid material we can hold in our hands. Primitive chondrites date to about 4.567 billion years — older than Earth itself. Studying them tells us about the conditions and ingredients present when the solar system was forming.
  • They are free samples from other worlds. Lunar and Martian meteorites give scientists material from the Moon and Mars without the enormous cost of a sample-return mission.
  • They contain the building blocks of life. Certain stony meteorites called carbonaceous chondrites contain water-bearing minerals, carbon compounds, and even amino acids — the building blocks of proteins. The famous Murchison meteorite that fell in Australia in 1969 contained over 70 different amino acids. This has profound implications for understanding how life's ingredients may have been delivered to early Earth.
  • ALH84001, a Martian meteorite found in Antarctica, caused worldwide excitement in 1996 when NASA scientists suggested it might contain microscopic structures resembling fossilised bacteria. The claim remains highly controversial and unresolved, but it sparked serious scientific debate about life on Mars.
Distinguishing a Meteorite from an Ordinary Rock

Many people find unusual-looking rocks and wonder if they're meteorites. Here are the key signs scientists look for:

  • Fusion crust: The dark, smooth outer shell described earlier.
  • Regmaglypts: Thumb-print-like depressions on the surface, formed as the outer material ablated (burned away) during atmospheric entry.
  • Magnetic attraction: Most meteorites (stony and iron types) contain iron or nickel and will stick to a strong magnet, unlike most common Earth rocks.
  • High density: Especially iron meteorites feel unusually heavy.
  • No bubbles or holes: Unlike many volcanic rocks (e.g., pumice), meteorites don't have a vesicular (bubbly) texture caused by trapped gas.
  • The Widmanstätten pattern (visible only in sliced and etched iron meteorites).
The Study of Meteorites

The scientific discipline dedicated to studying meteorites is called meteoritics. Scientists who specialise in this field are called meteoriticists. They work at the intersection of geology, chemistry, astronomy, and planetary science.

Summary in One Paragraph

A meteorite is a natural piece of rock or metal from outer space that survived a fiery entry through Earth's atmosphere and landed on the surface. It starts its life as a meteoroid (or asteroid fragment) in space, becomes a meteor (a visible streak of light) as it burns through the atmosphere, and earns the name meteorite upon landing. Meteorites are made of rock (stony), metal (iron), or a mix of both (stony-iron), and they come mostly from the asteroid belt, with some from the Moon and Mars. They range from microscopic dust to objects weighing tens of tonnes. They are scientifically priceless — the oldest solid objects we can physically study — and they have shaped life on Earth, both by delivering chemical building blocks billions of years ago, and occasionally by causing devastating impact events.
